title: Capstone 4: a parallel pipeline that survives failure
body: This capstone combines domains, ownership and error handling. The pipeline splits the input lines into contiguous chunks, gives each chunk to its own domain, lets each domain count words into a *private* hash table, and merges the tables on the main domain. Nothing mutable is shared while the workers run, so there is no lock and no race.

Failure is the hard part. If one worker raises, `Domain.join` re-raises that exception in the caller. If you join the domains one at a time and let the first exception escape, the remaining domains are never joined: they keep running in the background and their resources leak. The correct shape is to join *every* domain, capture each outcome as a `result`, and only then re-raise the first error.

Make cleanup observable. Each worker increments an `Atomic` counter in a `Fun.protect ~finally`, so a test can assert that all workers finished even though one failed. The same discipline applies to Async and effect-based code: every spawned unit of work is either awaited or cancelled, and the error path is tested as carefully as the success path.
challenge: src/pipeline.ml defines `default_process` and the `finished` counter, but `count` returns an empty list. Implement `count ~workers ?process lines`: chunk the lines, run one domain per chunk, count words into a private Hashtbl (incrementing `finished` in a `Fun.protect ~finally`), join every domain capturing `Ok`/`Error`, re-raise the first error after all are joined, and otherwise merge the tables into a list of (word, count) sorted by word. Reject `workers < 1` with `Invalid_argument`, and if spawning fails part-way, join the domains that already started before re-raising.
projectInstructions: Run `dune test --root .`. Edit only src/pipeline.ml. The test checks several worker counts, an empty input, and a worker that raises `Failure "boom"` while the other workers must still finish.
question: Why join every domain before re-raising a worker's exception?
correct: Otherwise the remaining domains are left running and unjoined, leaking work and resources on the error path
wrong: Domain.join never raises, so there is nothing to handle
Joining twice makes the result faster
reasoning: Structured concurrency means every spawned task is awaited; capturing outcomes first lets the caller clean up everything before reporting the failure.
